inputs.need:
I work in the environmental health team of a county health unit that covers about 180,000 people, a mix of small towns and farms. After two carbon monoxide deaths in rented farm cottages last winter, our board wants to know how many homes actually have a working carbon monoxide alarm and a working smoke alarm, and whether renters are worse off than owners. We want to run a cross-sectional household survey this winter to estimate the prevalence of working alarms by tenure and by main heating type (wood or coal, heating oil, bottled gas, heat pump), so that our alarm giveaway can be targeted instead of spread thin.

The fire service does home safety visits, but only when someone asks, so their records over-represent motivated households. We have the county property roll with every residential address but no tenure field. Our team has done telephone surveys before and response among renters and younger households was poor; door-to-door visits cost more but would let us press the test button and see where the alarm is.

I need help with the sampling frame, the sample size for comparing renters and owners, a definition of a working alarm (present, correctly sited, sounds when tested), what to do about refusals and addresses where nobody is home, and whether we need ethics review for a household survey that includes a brief look inside the home. I would also like to know what published evidence exists on alarm surveys in rural areas, because a colleague keeps quoting a figure of 40 percent that I cannot trace to any source.
inputs.constraints: Fieldwork budget of 18,000 for this winter. Fieldwork must finish by the end of March. No entry beyond the hallway or kitchen, and never without an adult householder present.
localFacts: The county property roll lists 71,400 residential addresses and has no tenure field.
The fire service completed 1,120 home safety visits last year, all made on request.
The health unit's research ethics committee meets monthly and has not reviewed a household survey with in-home observation before.

response.title: Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms by housing tenure in a rural county
response.subtitle: Cross-sectional household survey with test-button verification
response.statement: After two carbon monoxide deaths in rented farm cottages, the county health unit does not know how many homes have a working carbon monoxide alarm or a working smoke alarm, or whether renters are worse off than owners. A cross-sectional household survey this winter would estimate the prevalence of working alarms by tenure and heating type so that the alarm giveaway can be targeted.
response.whoAffected: Households in a rural county of about 180,000 people, especially renters in older farm cottages heated with solid fuel or bottled gas, and the environmental health team and fire service who run the alarm programme.
response.whatHurts: Carbon monoxide poisoning is silent and often fatal at night; alarms that are absent, badly sited or past their replacement date give no warning. The current giveaway reaches people who ask for home visits, who may be the households least at risk.
response.currentPractice: Alarms are fitted during fire service home safety visits made on request; the health unit has no population estimate of working alarms and relies on an untraced figure of 40 percent.
response.whyNow: Two deaths last winter, pressure from the board to act before the next heating season, and a fieldwork window that closes at the end of March.
response.constraints: Fieldwork budget of 18,000; fieldwork ends by the end of March; entry only to the hallway or kitchen with an adult householder present; the property roll has no tenure field.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Every household at risk of carbon monoxide exposure has a working, correctly sited alarm before the next heating season.
response.summary: Problem framed as a prevalence question by tenure and heating type, to target an existing alarm programme.

records.title: Working carbon monoxide alarms in rural households: a door-to-door survey with test-button verification
records.authors: Halloran-Pike S, Mensah-Ortiz D, Tveit-Adeyemi L
records.abstract: We drew a random sample of 1,140 rural addresses and visited each up to three times. At the 661 responding households (response 58 percent), fieldworkers asked about alarms and then pressed the test button. A carbon monoxide alarm sounded when tested in 37 percent of households, although 61 percent said they owned one. A working smoke alarm was found in 78 percent. Households heated with solid fuel were the least likely to have a working carbon monoxide alarm.

records.title: National housing condition survey 2019: smoke and carbon monoxide alarm module
records.abstract: The 2019 national housing condition survey inspected a stratified sample of dwellings. Surveyors recorded a working smoke alarm in 88 percent of dwellings and a carbon monoxide alarm in 44 percent of dwellings with a fuel-burning appliance, without a sound test for carbon monoxide alarms. Coverage was lowest in privately rented dwellings built before 1919.

records.title: Tenure and alarm functioning in rented rural housing: a cross-sectional study in two districts
records.abstract: In two rural districts we visited 820 sampled homes (response 49 percent) and tested alarms with the householder present. Working carbon monoxide alarms were present in 28 percent of privately rented homes and 44 percent of owner-occupied homes (prevalence ratio 0.64). The gap was largest in homes heated with bottled gas. Landlord-supplied alarms were more often past their replacement date.

records.title: Telephone versus door-to-door recruitment for household safety surveys: response and bias by tenure
records.abstract: We compared telephone and door-to-door recruitment for a household safety survey in the same sampled areas. Door-to-door recruitment reached 61 percent of sampled renters compared with 29 percent by telephone. After weighting, the telephone sample overstated the prevalence of working alarms by 9 percentage points.

records.title: Fire service home safety visits: who asks for them and who does not
records.venue: Fire and Rescue Service research note series
records.abstract: We compared households that requested a fire service home safety visit with the census profile of the areas they lived in. Requesting households were older and more often owner-occupied. Renters made up 12 percent of visits against 27 percent of households.

records.title: Carbon monoxide deaths in rural dwellings: a ten-year case series from coroners' records
records.abstract: We reviewed coroners' records of 41 accidental carbon monoxide deaths in rural dwellings over ten years. In 33 deaths the home had no working carbon monoxide alarm, and 24 involved solid fuel or bottled gas appliances. Rented dwellings were over-represented relative to the housing stock.

steps.note: Six records with abstracts; ids are stableRecordId values (see notes). Record 2 (the national survey) has no DOI, so its id comes from its title and year.

steps.responseText: I looked at the records you retrieved and at other studies of household carbon monoxide alarm ownership. In general, rural households appear less likely than urban ones to have a working alarm, and renters report fewer alarms than owners, although estimates vary widely between countries and survey methods. A door-to-door design with test-button verification is usually recommended over telephone questions because people overstate ownership when asked. I can format these findings as a structured evidence table with appraisal scores if that would help.

items.title: National housing condition survey 2019: smoke and carbon monoxide alarm module
items.keyFindings: Surveyors found a working smoke alarm in 88 percent of dwellings and a carbon monoxide alarm in 44 percent of dwellings with a fuel-burning appliance. Coverage was lowest in privately rented dwellings built before 1919.
items.limitations: National figures dominated by urban housing; carbon monoxide alarms were recorded as present without a sound test.

items.title: Predictors of smoke and carbon monoxide alarm ownership: a systematic review of household surveys
items.authors: Kristiansen-Obi M, Laurent-Achebe P, Duarte-Hollis C
items.keyFindings: Across 26 household surveys, renting, lower income and older housing were the most consistent predictors of not owning a working alarm. Self-reported ownership exceeded verified ownership by 15 to 30 percentage points in the eight surveys that measured both.
items.limitations: Mostly urban surveys; heterogeneous definitions of a working alarm; no pooled estimate for rural areas.
items.notes: Supports tenure as the main stratifier.

items.title: Landlord compliance with alarm regulations in private rented housing: an inspection audit
items.keyFindings: Inspectors found a working carbon monoxide alarm next to the fuel-burning appliance in 46 percent of inspected rented homes where one was legally required. Non-compliance was higher where the landlord owned a single property.
items.limitations: Urban inspection sample chosen after complaints; no owner-occupied comparison.
items.notes: Relevant to why rented homes may lack alarms.

items.title: Visual carbon monoxide alarms for householders with hearing loss: a small survey of use and acceptability
items.keyFindings: Among 64 householders with hearing loss, most could not hear a standard alarm from the bedroom, and 49 of 64 kept a visual alarm fitted six months later.
items.limitations: Small convenience sample recruited through one support group.
items.notes: Informs the equity element of the giveaway.

items.title: Seasonal carbon monoxide concentrations in homes heated with bottled gas: a measurement study
items.keyFindings: Winter indoor carbon monoxide peaks above the short-term guideline value were recorded in 9 of 58 homes heated with portable bottled gas heaters and in none of 40 comparison homes.
items.limitations: Small sample; one winter; heater age not recorded.
items.notes: Supports heating type as a second stratifier.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Tested working carbon monoxide alarms are much less common than reported ownership (37 against 61 percent in one rural survey), rented homes had fewer working alarms than owner-occupied homes in two rural districts (28 against 44 percent), and door-to-door recruitment reached renters far better than telephone. A national survey recorded carbon monoxide alarms in 44 percent of dwellings with a fuel-burning appliance without testing them. The 40 percent figure quoted locally matches no retrieved record.
response.gradeRationale: Descriptive surveys with moderate response from a few areas, a national survey without sound tests, and grey service data; consistent in direction but imprecise for this county.

response.reading: Tenure and heating type shape both the risk of carbon monoxide exposure and the chance of having a working alarm, while the only existing local data (fire service visits) come from households who ask. A probability sample from the property roll with verification at the door is the only way to see the households the current programme misses. Self-report is the main measurement trap, and one model lead tried to pass a retrieved national survey off as a landmark with an invented identifier.

response.overview: Cross-sectional household survey from January to March 2027 with door-to-door visits and test-button verification of alarms, drawn as a stratified two-stage cluster sample from the county property roll.
response.population: Occupied residential addresses on the county property roll; one adult householder per address; tenure recorded at the door.
response.exposure: Housing tenure (privately rented, social rented, owner-occupied) and main heating type (solid fuel, heating oil, bottled gas, heat pump or electric).
response.procedures: Seventy segments of about 23 addresses each are selected with probability proportional to size within town and rural strata, giving about 1,630 addresses. Fieldworkers in pairs visit up to three times at different times of day. With verbal consent they record alarm presence, siting, manufacture date and whether the alarm sounds when the test button is pressed, in the hallway and kitchen only. Households with a fuel-burning appliance and no working carbon monoxide alarm are offered a free alarm fitted by the fire service within two weeks.

response.designSummary: Stratified two-stage cluster sample; survey-weighted prevalence estimates and a prevalence ratio for renters versus owners.
response.sampleSize: Planning values: a working carbon monoxide alarm in 45 percent of owner-occupied and 30 percent of rented homes with a fuel-burning appliance. Detecting that 15-point difference with 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 needs 163 households per group; with a design effect of 1.5 for clustering this becomes 245 per group. Renters are about a quarter of households, so about 980 completed households are needed to reach 245 renters. With 60 percent response, about 1,630 addresses are sampled. The overall prevalence will then have a 95 percent confidence interval of about 3.8 percentage points either side at a prevalence of 40 percent.
response.primaryAnalysis: Survey-weighted prevalence of a working carbon monoxide alarm by tenure, with design weights for selection probability and nonresponse adjustment by segment and dwelling type; prevalence ratio for privately rented versus owner-occupied homes from a weighted Poisson model with robust variance that accounts for clustering.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Prevalence ratio adjusted for heating type, dwelling age, household size and rural or town stratum; prevalence by heating type; agreement between reported and working alarms; the same estimates for smoke alarms.
response.missingData: Unit nonresponse is handled by weighting classes; households that refuse the test are reported separately, and bounds are given by treating untested alarms first as working and then as not working.
response.multiplicity: One primary comparison; secondary estimates are reported with confidence intervals and no significance claims.
response.software: R with the survey package; weights and code archived before fieldwork ends.
overfittingGuards: Planning values and design effect recorded before sampling
response.summary: About 1,630 addresses for 980 completed visits give 80 percent power for a 15-point tenure difference after a design effect of 1.5.

response.risks: Low: a short doorstep interview and a look at alarms in the hallway and kitchen. Risks are intrusion, fieldworker safety in isolated places, and renters worrying that findings reach landlords.
response.consent: Verbal informed consent at the door after an information sheet, recorded by the fieldworker; separate consent for entering the hallway or kitchen; the householder may stop at any point.
response.data: Addresses are held separately from responses and linked only by a segment code; no data are shared with landlords; the fire service receives an address only when the householder asks for a fitted alarm.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: renters, low-income households, seasonal agricultural workers with limited English, older people living alone and people with hearing loss are the groups most likely to lack a working alarm or to be unable to hear one. Materials are offered in the main local languages, fieldworkers carry alarms with visual alerts, and results are reported by tenure and heating type.
response.effectiveness: The survey decides where the giveaway goes; its value depends on the renter comparison being precise enough to change targeting.
response.efficiency: Door-to-door verification costs more than telephone questions but measures the outcome directly; it fits the budget.
response.costs: About 17,900 for fieldwork, travel and alarms for households found without one; analysis within existing staff time.
response.grants: None needed for this winter; a proactive fitting programme could seek regional funding afterwards.
response.partnerships: Fire service (fitting and safety training), a tenants' association, a farmworker support organisation, and the landlords' association for dissemination.
response.rebPath: Review by the health unit's research ethics committee before fieldwork; the committee meets monthly and has not reviewed a survey with in-home observation before, so the decision is unknown. Consent and confidentiality follow ICH-GCP principles.
response.limitations: Nonresponse may still differ by tenure; alarms in bedrooms are not inspected; one winter only.
response.summary: Low-risk survey with verbal consent, an obligation to offer an alarm when none works, and an ethics decision that is still unknown.

response.partnershipPlan: A tenants' association and a farmworker support organisation review the doorstep script and the information sheet; the fire service trains fieldworkers; results are shared with the board and the landlords' association.
response.socialListening: A three-month read of the county community forum and the local radio phone-in summaries for mentions of alarms and heating, recorded as composites without names.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: I would not tell anyone the alarm is broken in case the landlord hears I complained.
items.implication: Keep a strict rule of no sharing with landlords and state it on the information sheet.

items.theme: Not knowing what the alarm is for
items.quote: Composite paraphrase: There is a white box in the kitchen but I thought that was for smoke.
items.implication: Record alarm type at the door and explain the difference when offering a fitted alarm.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: The people who ring us already have three alarms; the ones we worry about never call.
items.implication: Use survey segments with the lowest prevalence to plan proactive visits.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: Anyone in a lanyard knocking in winter, I am not opening the door.
items.implication: Announce fieldwork through the forum and local radio and give a number to check fieldworker identity.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: Every winter we see families with headaches that turn out to be the boiler.
items.implication: Add a short symptom leaflet to the visit for households with fuel-burning appliances.

response.summary: Five composite voices on landlord fear, alarm confusion, visit selection, doorstep distrust and unrecognised symptoms.

response.title: Working carbon monoxide and smoke alarms by housing tenure in a rural county: a cross-sectional household survey with test-button verification
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the prevalence of working carbon monoxide and smoke alarms by housing tenure and heating type in a rural county. Design: cross-sectional household survey from a stratified two-stage cluster sample of the property roll, January to March 2027, with test-button verification. Primary outcome: a working carbon monoxide alarm in homes with a fuel-burning appliance. Results and conclusions will be written after fieldwork.
response.introduction: Carbon monoxide deaths cluster in homes without a working alarm, and existing local data come only from households who ask for fire service visits. Retrieved surveys suggest that renters and homes heated with solid fuel or bottled gas are least protected, but no estimate by tenure exists for this county.
response.methods: About 1,630 addresses in 70 segments are sampled with probability proportional to size within town and rural strata. Fieldworkers visit up to three times, record reported ownership, then test alarms in the hallway and kitchen. Survey-weighted prevalence and a prevalence ratio for rented versus owner-occupied homes are estimated with robust variance.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present response by tenure, weighted prevalence with confidence intervals by tenure and heating type, the renter and owner prevalence ratio, and agreement between reported and working alarms.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare the county estimates with the retrieved rural and national figures, weigh nonresponse bias, and set out how the giveaway will be retargeted.
response.limitations: Nonresponse may differ by tenure; bedrooms are not inspected; tenure is reported at the door; one winter only.
response.conclusion: To be written after fieldwork; it will be limited to prevalence and the tenure comparison and will not claim effects of the giveaway.
response.summary: STROBE-structured draft with results left empty until fieldwork ends.
